prompt_free_text:
This paper studies an important and timely problem: how a user can determine whether a black-box LLM API is actually serving the same distribution as a claimed reference model, or whether it has been altered through quantization, watermarking, finetuning, implementation differences, or silent updates. The paper formalizes this as a two-sample hypothesis testing problem, proposes MMD-based tests with string kernels, and argues empirically that a simple Hamming kernel is particularly effective in the low-sample regime. It then applies the method to commercial APIs serving Llama-family models and reports that a substantial fraction of endpoints appear statistically distinguishable from Meta’s released weights.

Overall, I found the paper interesting, practically relevant, and stronger than many purely anecdotal API auditing studies. The framing is clean, the methodology is sensible, and the empirical audit of real providers is compelling. The paper’s main contribution is not a fundamentally new statistical test, but rather a careful problem formulation, a convincing adaptation of kernel two-sample testing to LLM outputs, and an application that exposes meaningful discrepancies in deployed systems. I think this is a valuable contribution for the community, especially given the increasing reliance on opaque inference APIs.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the problem formulation. “Model Equality Testing” is a useful abstraction that unifies several concerns that are often discussed separately: verifying faithfulness to open weights, detecting API drift over time, and identifying model substitution. Casting these as two-sample testing over prompt-completion pairs is natural and gives the work a principled statistical foundation. I also appreciated that the paper emphasizes user-centric auditing on custom prompt distributions rather than benchmark-only evaluation. This is a meaningful shift from current practice.

The methodological choice is also well motivated. In this setting, exact multinomial tests over full completions are hopelessly sparse, and the paper correctly argues that the kernel choice determines whether one can extract useful low-dimensional structure from samples. The empirical comparison between one-hot, all-substrings, Hamming, and classical multinomial closeness statistics supports the claim that the Hamming kernel is a good bias-variance tradeoff in the small-sample regime. The decomposition with prompt-matching kernels is simple and elegant. The paper is also commendably honest that the Hamming MMD is only a pseudometric and may miss some differences.

The empirical section is generally strong. The simulation suite covers several realistic distortions: quantization, watermarking, finetuning, and model substitution. The headline result that around 10 samples per prompt can already yield useful power is practically important. The real-world audit is the most compelling part of the paper. Finding that 11 of 31 endpoints differ from the reference distribution is a striking result, and the observation that discrepancies are larger on specialized domains than on generic Wikipedia continuation is plausible and useful. The release of code and a large completion dataset also improves the paper’s value.

That said, I have several concerns, mostly around interpretation, statistical calibration, and the limits of the chosen kernel.

My main conceptual concern is that the paper sometimes slides between “distribution differs” and “provider modified the model” too quickly. A rejection only establishes that the sampled output distribution under the tested protocol differs from the chosen reference distribution. This could arise from many causes besides quantization or finetuning: undocumented system prompts, prompt formatting differences, tokenizer/version mismatches, stop-sequence handling, sampling implementation details, temperature/top-p clipping, repetition penalties, safety filters, semantic caching, load-balancing across model variants, or even nondeterministic backend changes over time. The paper acknowledges some of these possibilities, but the presentation of the audit results could more carefully distinguish “endpoint is not distributionally identical under our protocol” from stronger causal claims about what the provider did. This is especially important because the title and framing invite forensic interpretation.

Relatedly, the null hypothesis assumes the same vocabulary and decoding parameters, but in practice commercial APIs often do not expose or implement these identically. In Section 5 the authors move to character-space testing because APIs return decoded text, which is reasonable, but this also changes the semantics of equality. Two token-level distributions can differ while inducing similar character-level outputs, and vice versa due to whitespace normalization, Unicode handling, or tokenizer-specific segmentation artifacts. The paper should discuss more explicitly what notion of equality is actually being tested in the API audit: equality of decoded string distributions under a particular client-side protocol, not equality of underlying token distributions. That is still useful, but narrower and more operational than the broader framing suggests.

A second concern is statistical calibration in the real audit. The paper says tests are run at level alpha = 0.01 with N = 10m samples, repeated over ten samples, and endpoints are failed if the average rejection rate is at least 0.5. This “majority vote over repeated tests” is intuitively variance-reducing, but it is not obvious that it preserves a clean family-wise or per-endpoint Type I error guarantee, especially under dependence induced by shared prompts, shared null samples, or temporal drift during collection. The paper gives a valid argument for the composite null rule requiring both p1 and p2 < alpha, but I did not see a similarly rigorous treatment of the repeated-testing-and-thresholding procedure. If the endpoint-level decision rule is central to the headline “11 out of 31 endpoints” claim, then its false positive properties should be characterized explicitly, ideally by simulation under the null. Otherwise, the audit results are harder to interpret.

A related issue is multiple testing. The paper audits many endpoints across multiple prompt distributions and sometimes combines results with Bonferroni in Figure 1, but Table 1 appears to report per-task failures without a global multiplicity correction across all endpoints and tasks. That may be acceptable if the goal is descriptive auditing rather than confirmatory claims, but the paper should be clearer about which claims are controlled at what error rate. As written, readers may over-interpret the number of flagged endpoints as if it were globally calibrated.

Third, while the Hamming kernel works well empirically, its limitations deserve more scrutiny. Because it only counts position-wise token or character matches, it is sensitive to surface-form changes but blind to many semantically meaningful differences and many distributional changes that preserve marginal token identities at positions. The paper notes reduced power against fp16, which is already evidence that the kernel misses some subtle shifts. More broadly, if two models differ mainly in long-range dependencies, paraphrastic variation, or latent reasoning trajectories while preserving local token statistics, the Hamming kernel may have poor power. Conversely, it may overreact to benign formatting differences. I would have liked a more systematic analysis of failure modes, perhaps with synthetic alternatives designed to preserve Hamming statistics while changing higher-order structure, or vice versa.

Fourth, the prompt distributions used in simulation are somewhat narrow. The Wikipedia continuation setup with random 100-character prefixes is a convenient long-form generation task, but it is not obvious that it represents the kinds of prompts users care about most. The paper partially addresses this by adding HumanEval and UltraChat in the API audit, which is good, but the simulation-based kernel selection is still largely driven by Wikipedia continuation. Since the central claim is that the Hamming MMD generalizes across tasks and models, it would strengthen the paper to include more diverse prompt distributions in the controlled experiments, such as instruction following, summarization, dialogue, or retrieval-grounded prompts.

Fifth, the comparison to alternative tests is useful but not fully exhaustive. Since the paper’s main empirical claim is that Hamming-MMD is especially powerful, it would be helpful to compare against stronger baselines from modern representation-based testing. For example, one could embed completions using a pretrained encoder or LM hidden states and run MMD or energy distance in embedding space. Even simple n-gram TF-IDF embeddings or edit-distance kernels might be competitive. The current baselines are mostly exact-string or classical multinomial tests, which are expected to struggle in sparse high-dimensional regimes. The paper’s conclusion that “a simple string kernel works best” is plausible, but it would be more convincing against a broader set of semantic or representation-aware baselines.

I also have some concerns about the interpretation of estimated MMD as an “effect size” across models and providers. Since the Hamming MMD depends strongly on prompt distribution, output length, decoding protocol, and representation space, cross-comparison of absolute values can be misleading. Statements like “some APIs are further from the reference than an entirely different language model” are striking, but they should be qualified carefully: this is with respect to this kernel, this prompt distribution, and this sampling setup. I do not think the paper is wrong to make such comparisons, but it should avoid implying a universal notion of model distance.

There are also a few smaller technical and presentation issues. The paper should clarify whether null simulations for p-values reuse the same prompt draws or resample prompts from pi each time; this matters because the test is over joint prompt-completion pairs. It would also help to report confidence intervals more consistently for power estimates and endpoint rejection rates. The computational cost of the all-substrings kernel is mentioned as expensive, but actual runtime comparisons would be useful. Some of the strongest claims in the audit section would benefit from temporal replication, since API behavior can drift; a single collection window may conflate persistent provider differences with transient backend states. Finally, the conflict of interest is disclosed, which is good, but given that Together is one of the audited providers and is reported as passing all tests, it would be reassuring to know whether any additional safeguards were used in data collection or analysis.

Despite these concerns, I think the paper makes a meaningful contribution. The core idea is sound, the empirical evidence is substantial, and the real-world audit is likely to be impactful. The work opens a useful line of research on black-box model verification that is more statistically principled than benchmark spot-checking. I would lean positive on acceptance, provided the authors tighten the claims and better characterize the statistical properties of the endpoint-level audit procedure.

The paper would be significantly strengthened by the following revisions. First, sharpen the interpretation of the audit results: emphasize that the test detects distributional non-identity under a specified prompting and decoding protocol, not necessarily the exact cause or internal modification. Second, provide a formal or empirical analysis of the repeated-test decision rule used in Section 5, including its effective false positive rate under realistic dependence. Third, clarify the scope of multiple-testing control across endpoints and tasks. Fourth, add at least one stronger baseline using embedding-space or semantic representations. Fifth, expand the discussion of failure modes of the Hamming kernel and perhaps include one controlled experiment where it is expected to fail. Sixth, qualify the use of MMD as an effect size and avoid over-generalizing absolute distances across settings.

In summary, this is a strong and timely paper with clear practical relevance, a principled formulation, and compelling real-world findings. Its main weaknesses are not fatal, but they matter because the paper’s conclusions could otherwise be over-interpreted. With clearer statistical accounting and more careful framing, I think this work would be a valuable addition to a top-tier ML conference.

prompt_structured_json.summary: This paper formulates auditing black-box LLM APIs as a two-sample hypothesis testing problem called Model Equality Testing. Given samples from a reference model distribution and an API distribution over prompt-completion pairs, the goal is to test whether the two conditional output distributions are equal. The authors propose using MMD-based kernel two-sample tests, with a simple Hamming string kernel over completions as the main practical choice. Through simulations on quantization, watermarking, finetuning, and model substitution, they show that the Hamming-MMD test often has substantially higher power than one-hot, substring, and multinomial baselines in low-sample regimes. They then apply the method to 31 commercial endpoints serving Llama-family models and report that 11 endpoints appear statistically different from Meta reference weights/fp16 variants, with larger deviations on some domain-specific tasks. The paper also uses estimated MMD values as an effect-size notion for comparing models and providers.
strengths: Timely and practically important problem: black-box API auditing for LLMs is highly relevant for reproducibility, benchmarking, and user trust.
Clear formalization of API auditing as a two-sample testing problem over prompt-completion distributions.
Method is conceptually simple, broadly applicable, and does not require log-probability access, making it realistic for commercial APIs.
Empirical study is fairly extensive: multiple distortions (quantization, watermarking, finetuning, model swaps), multiple models, and a real-world audit of commercial providers.
The Hamming-kernel MMD choice is computationally simple and appears empirically effective in low-sample settings, especially relative to exact-match/multinomial baselines.
The paper goes beyond binary testing by using estimated MMD as a distance/effect-size proxy, which is useful for exploratory auditing.
Open-sourcing code and a large completion dataset increases reproducibility and potential impact.
weaknesses: The main method relies on a non-characteristic kernel (Hamming), so failure to reject does not imply equality, and even estimated distances can be zero for distinct distributions; this weakens the semantic interpretation of 'model equality' in the title.

The empirical validation is strong but largely heuristic; there is limited theory explaining when the Hamming kernel should be powerful against realistic LLM distortions or how power scales with prompt diversity, completion length, and sample size.

The prompt distributions used in simulation are somewhat artificial (random Wikipedia prefixes across languages), which may not reflect many real deployment settings; conclusions about generality may therefore be overstated.

The API audit conclusions may be confounded by uncontrolled implementation differences beyond model weights, such as tokenizer/version mismatches, hidden system prompts, safety filters, stop-sequence handling, sampling stack differences, or undocumented decoding defaults.

The decision rule for API auditing averages rejection rates over ten repeated tests and declares failure if the average rejection rate is at least 0.5; this is unusual and its statistical operating characteristics are not rigorously justified.

The paper emphasizes power but gives relatively limited direct empirical calibration evidence for Type-I error control in the exact practical settings used for API audits, especially under character-space comparisons and repeated-testing heuristics.

Comparisons across providers in character space may mix model differences with formatting artifacts, whitespace normalization, Unicode handling, or truncation behavior, which could inflate measured discrepancies.
Some claims about practical severity (e.g., an API being 'further than another language model') depend on a pseudometric whose scale and semantic meaning are not fully grounded.
methodological_flaws: The composite-null testing argument in Section 5 is only partially satisfactory. While the rule 'reject iff p1<alpha and p2<alpha' does upper-bound FPR by alpha under the union null, the practical procedure actually repeats tests ten times and thresholds the average rejection rate at 0.5. The paper does not provide a formal proof that this repeated-sampling decision rule preserves the claimed overall Type-I error level.

The use of simulated null draws from the reference model for p-values assumes the reference sampling process exactly matches the null distribution of interest. In API audits, however, the comparison is performed in character space and may involve preprocessing/decoding transformations not mirrored perfectly between reference and API outputs, potentially violating exchangeability or null calibration assumptions.

The central empirical claim that Hamming-MMD is the best practical test is based on a restricted baseline set. Stronger alternatives from modern kernel testing or sequence embedding approaches (e.g., learned embeddings, spectrum kernels with tuning, energy distance on embeddings, classifier two-sample tests) are not evaluated, so the superiority claim is only relative to limited baselines.

Because the Hamming kernel is not characteristic, the test is not consistent against all alternatives. This is acknowledged, but the paper still frames the task as testing model equality in general. Scientifically, the method only tests equality with respect to the chosen feature geometry, not full distributional equality, unless stronger kernels are used.

The API audit may suffer from hidden nuisance variables: if providers alter prompts, inject templates, or enforce moderation/safety transformations, the observed rejection does not isolate model-weight distortion. Thus the causal interpretation 'which model is this API serving?' is stronger than what the experiment strictly identifies.

The reported correlation between MMD and HumanEval accuracy difference is modest (R^2=0.392), yet some discussion risks implying stronger practical alignment between statistical distance and capability difference than is warranted.
